title: An American Engineer in China
gist: A new Not Boring 'Field Notes' series follows a pseudonymous American engineer ('Matthew') touring Hong Kong and Shenzhen, arguing China's economy is pivoting from copycat manufacturing/investing to owning brands, deeptech strategy, and vertically integrated energy infrastructure, while foreigners remain structurally locked out of local manufacturing networks.

insights.claim: China's economy is shifting from contract manufacturing to owning consumer brands, from copying US VC playbooks to running state-backed deeptech investment strategies, and from single-product battery cell makers to companies that own grid and datacenter assets — investors still modeling China on its prior decade's playbook risk being blindsided.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Investors benchmarking Chinese industrials/energy companies against their old OEM/battery-supplier identity are underpricing their move up the value chain into branded consumer goods, deeptech capital allocation, and energy-asset ownership.
insights.quote: The China of 2036 will be vastly different than the China of 2026.

insights.claim: Companies that once manufactured luxury handbags for Western labels in China are now launching and building their own branded product lines rather than remaining anonymous contract manufacturers.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Western luxury and consumer brands sourcing from Chinese factories should expect their own suppliers to emerge as direct competitors, not just cost-plus vendors.

insights.claim: Chinese investors who previously copied American VC models are now running their own state-backed deeptech investment playbooks distinct from the Silicon Valley template.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Western VCs benchmarking Chinese deeptech deal flow against their own playbook may misjudge underwriting criteria and timelines that are shaped by state industrial policy rather than pure market signals.

insights.claim: Chinese battery-cell manufacturers are vertically integrating downstream to become owners of grid assets and datacenters rather than remaining pure component suppliers.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Battery makers moving into owning downstream energy and compute infrastructure changes the competitive set for grid-storage and datacenter-power investors — the same firms may soon be customers, competitors, and suppliers simultaneously.

insights.claim: Beijing plans to spend over a trillion dollars on new domestic infrastructure over the next decade as part of a longer-run effort to restore China's position as the world's dominant civilization.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A trillion-dollar-plus decade-long domestic infrastructure buildout implies sustained demand for construction, materials, energy equipment, and industrial automation suppliers serving the Chinese market.
insights.quote: They’re going to spend over a trillion dollars on new infrastructure through the next decade
insights.locator: we are not at the center of their universe

insights.claim: Hong Kong has roughly 4,000 buildings above 100 meters tall, versus about 900 in New York City, America's densest city — a vertical building-stock density with no real US analog.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: This kind of density-driven scale (construction, real estate, transit, retail throughput) is a structural feature that Western urban markets cannot replicate, and it underpins downstream demand for elevators, HVAC, construction materials, and vertical logistics.

insights.claim: China's Greater Bay Area megaregion (Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau) has more skyscrapers than all of North America and Europe combined.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The physical build-out scale of a single Chinese megaregion already exceeds two continents combined, a baseline investors should use when sizing addressable markets for construction, energy, and infrastructure plays tied to China.
insights.locator: we are not at the center of their universe

insights.claim: Over 80% of people in China do not hold a college degree, undercutting narratives that frame China's technological rise as purely an elite, STEM-credentialed phenomenon.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: China's industrial and manufacturing base runs largely on a non-college-educated workforce, meaning labor-cost and skill assumptions used in Western competitiveness comparisons should be checked against this reality rather than an assumed engineering-heavy talent pyramid.
insights.quote: Over 80% of people in China do not hold a college degree.

themes.theme: Foreigners Are Structurally Locked Out of Manufacturing

insights.claim: There are essentially no foreigner-run ODMs (Original Design Manufacturers) in Shenzhen because foreign operators never qualify for the government subsidies available to local players and get systematically outcompeted, regardless of language fluency or years of residency.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Western firms trying to build owned manufacturing operations in Shenzhen rather than partnering with local suppliers are fighting a subsidy-driven cost disadvantage that is effectively permanent, not merely a learning-curve problem.

insights.claim: Foreign buyers who evaluate Chinese manufacturing costs on simple input/output economics rather than full process knowledge get overcharged; one supplier reportedly charged a foreign company $200,000 for a machine that should have cost $20,000.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Due diligence on Chinese supply-chain cost quotes needs process-level cost breakdowns, not headline landed-cost comparisons — a 10x markup gap is plausible for buyers who skip that step.
insights.quote: He’s seen suppliers charge companies $200k for a machine that should have cost $20k.

insights.claim: IP protection is a live, ongoing operational risk when working with Shenzhen-based suppliers given how intensely competitive the local supplier ecosystem is.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Foreign companies sourcing hardware from Shenzhen should assume IP leakage risk as a baseline cost of doing business, not an edge case, and structure contracts/process disclosure accordingly.

themes.theme: Robotics and Automation Ahead of Outside Perception

insights.claim: A commercially deployed dual-arm robot, the Galbot S1, was observed lifting 50kg with both arms in a Shenzhen retail/public setting, indicating embodied-AI hardware in China is already visible outside lab or factory demos.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Humanoid/dual-arm robot capability that Western observers associate with demo videos is already in public-facing deployment in China, a leading indicator for how fast embodied-AI hardware could scale into logistics and retail labor.

insights.claim: Meituan already operates dedicated drone-delivery takeoff infrastructure but has not fully automated food delivery with drones despite having the technical capability, reportedly because replacing the human delivery workforce at scale would risk social unrest.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The binding constraint on last-mile delivery automation in China may be social/political stability risk rather than technology readiness — a factor that could delay Meituan's automation rollout timeline versus what the hardware alone would suggest.
insights.quote: if Meituan tried replacing them all with drone delivery, there would be so many riots in the streets.

insights.claim: Bambu Lab's flagship Shenzhen store openly advertises that its 3D printers can manufacture guns, highlighting a stark regulatory and cultural gap versus the US, where 3D-printed 'ghost guns' are a politically fraught, restricted category.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Consumer hardware companies like Bambu Lab operate under materially different regulatory permission structures at home versus in the US, which matters for how they market products and for US policy scrutiny of Chinese-made 3D printers.
insights.locator: I went to the original Bambu Labs store

themes.theme: Political Geography: Shenzhen Ascendant, Hong Kong Eclipsed

insights.claim: Hong Kong's historic dominance as China's financial hub, built on a favorable tax structure and lighter regulation than the mainland, has eroded as COVID-era rule changes pushed foreign capital and talent toward Singapore while Shanghai, Beijing, and Shenzhen grew rapidly since the 1990s.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Hong Kong's relative decline as a financial center versus Singapore and mainland hubs is a multi-year structural trend, not a cyclical dip, relevant to anyone allocating financial-services or holding-company infrastructure across Asia.

insights.claim: APEC 2026, traditionally hosted in Beijing or Shanghai, is being held in Shenzhen for the first time, a deliberate signal from Xi Jinping elevating the city's political and economic status.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Hosting APEC in Shenzhen is a concrete, watchable signal of Beijing formally elevating Shenzhen's status as China's hardware/tech capital on the world stage, ahead of similar diplomatic showcases.
insights.quote: APEC 2026, normally held in Beijing/Shanghai, is being held here for the first time because Xi likes the city and the government wants to show it off.

insights.claim: Genuine Nvidia GPUs (including a 5090) circulate through Shenzhen's Huaqiangbei gray-market electronics bazaar identical to the US retail product, showing high-end US silicon still reaches Chinese retail channels despite export-control tensions.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: On-the-ground availability of current-generation Nvidia GPUs in Chinese consumer electronics markets is a real-time gray-market indicator worth tracking alongside official export-control compliance data.
insights.quote: The 5090 GPU I found in an electronics market here, though, was very much the same Nvidia as the US one.

insights.claim: Despite China's overwhelming domestic EV adoption, Tesla remains a visibly common brand on Shenzhen roads, indicating persistent Western EV brand equity even in the world's most EV-saturated consumer market.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Tesla's continued visible presence on the street in a market dominated by BYD-class domestic EVs suggests its brand hasn't been fully displaced, a data point against a total-wipeout thesis for Tesla in China.
insights.locator: Most people who drive are in EVs

insights.claim: Not Boring is launching a paid 'Field Notes' series written pseudonymously by an operator ('Matthew') embedded in China covering energy, AI, hardware, and manufacturing, distinct from existing China-watch outlets like Sinocism, ChinaTalk, Tech Buzz China, Hello China Tech, and Dan Wang's book Breakneck.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The launch of a paid, operator-sourced China intelligence product signals rising investor appetite for ground-truth, non-consensus China coverage on hardware and energy beyond existing analyst/journalist commentary.
